title: She Said, He Told Me
overview: This unit is about passing on what somebody else said. You will report a statement, an instruction and a piece of news you were given. You will learn when to use say and when to use tell. You will also ask somebody to do a job for you, add the time words a report needs, and work out what six everyday sayings mean.
learningPath: Meet 28 words for news, reporting, time and everyday sayings.
Read a short dialogue, an information page and a real message slip.
Learn said that and told me that, and how the verb steps back.
Pass on an instruction: She told me to wait.
Choose between say and tell, and add inform for a formal notice.
Ask through somebody else, and list the jobs you still have to do.
Add the time words: the day before, later that week, straight away.
Speak, write, check every answer against the key, then take the quiz and record the assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 17. This unit is about passing on what somebody else said.
Every day somebody gives you a message. A shop assistant, a neighbour, a person at a desk.
Later you have to pass it on. That is called reporting, and English has a plain way to do it.
Start with the words.
A statement is one thing a person says, said clearly and on purpose.
News is what has just happened. The word takes no plural s. We say the news is good.
A report is a longer account of what happened, written or spoken.
An announcement is news said out loud to a lot of people at one moment.
A headline is the short line at the top of a news story. It carries the subject and nothing else.
A rumour is a story going round that nobody has checked.
A source is the person or the place a piece of news came from.
A version is one person's account of an event. Two people can give two versions and both be honest.
Now the verbs for saying and telling.
Inform is the formal word for tell. You will see it on notices and in offices.
Remind means tell somebody again about something they already knew.
Complain means say that something is wrong.
Claim means say something is true when nobody has checked it yet.
Reply means answer. Argue means say the opposite, with a reason.
Announce means say it out loud so that everybody hears it.
Persuade means talk to somebody until they change their mind.
Now the pattern. This is the heart of the unit.
A person says a sentence. You want to pass it on.
Direct: The shop is shut.
Reported: She said that the shop was shut.
Two things change. You add said that. And the verb steps back one step in time.
Is becomes was. Are becomes were. Opens becomes opened. Will becomes would. Can becomes could.
The reported sentence takes no quotation marks, because they are no longer the person's exact words.
Now the difference between the two verbs.
Say does not take a person after it. Tell does.
She said that the shop was shut. She told me that the shop was shut.
Never: she said me. Never: she told that.
Now an instruction.
Direct: Wait here.
Reported: She told me to wait here.
Told, then the person, then to, then the plain verb.
If the instruction was negative, put not in front of to. She told me not to press it.
Use asked for a polite request: he asked me to ring again on Friday.
Next, asking through somebody else.
I need you to sign it. She wants me to come early. They asked him to wait.
The shape is the same every time: verb, person, to, plain verb.
And when you list a job that is still waiting, use have.
I have three calls to make. I have a form to fill in. I have nothing to do today.
Last, the time words.
A report almost always says when. A report with no time in it is hard to check.
Once you are reporting, the time word moves with you.
Yesterday becomes the day before. Tomorrow becomes the next day, or the following day.
Straight away means at once, with nothing in between.
Previous means the one before. Following means the one after.
Recent means not long ago. Current means now.
Former means before, and not now. Immediate means with no wait at all.
Six everyday sayings finish the unit.
Make up your mind means decide.
Keep an eye on means watch something while you do other things.
Run out of means have none of it left.
Take your time means do not hurry.
On purpose means you meant to do it. By mistake means you did not.
You cannot work a saying out from its separate words, so learn each one whole.
Now go to the words, then the five cards, then the practice. Every answer is inside the unit.

outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 2 practice, seven of eight; Practice 4, five of six; Speaking 2 recording played back and checked.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can tell somebody what I was asked or told to do.

outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 3 practice, seven of eight; Practice 2, seven of eight; comprehension question 7.

words.meaning: Something a person says or writes, said clearly and on purpose.
words.example: Her statement was short and clear.
practice: The driver gave a short statement about the delay.
That statement is easy to check.
He wrote his statement on one page.
Which statement did you believe?
words.tutor: Read me four short statements about a shop, one at a time, and I will say each one back starting with You said that.

words.meaning: What has just happened, told to other people. The word takes no plural s.
words.example: The news came on Monday.
practice: I have some news about the delivery date.
Is there any news from the office?
The news about the bus route is good.
She heard the news from a neighbour.
words.tutor: Give me one piece of ordinary news about a shop, then ask me to report it back with She said that.

words.meaning: A longer account of what happened, spoken or written.
words.example: The report was two pages long.
practice: The report gives the time and the place.
I read the report before I replied.
Her report says the bus route changed on Monday.
Who wrote this report?
words.tutor: Ask me three questions about a short report on a late delivery, and check that my answers use said that.

words.meaning: News said out loud to many people at one moment.
words.example: The announcement came over the speaker.
practice: There was an announcement about the late train.
Did you hear the announcement?
The shop put an announcement on the door.
The announcement lasted ten seconds.
words.tutor: Say a short station announcement to me, then ask me to report it with They announced that.

words.meaning: The short line at the top of a news story, giving the subject and nothing else.
words.example: The headline was only five words.
practice: I read the headline and then the story.
The headline says the bridge is open again.
A headline uses very few words.
Which headline tells you most?
words.tutor: Give me a five-word headline about a bus route, and I will write the first sentence of the story under it.

words.meaning: A story going round that nobody has checked.
words.example: It is only a rumour.
practice: A rumour went round that the café was closing.
Check a rumour before you pass it on.
That rumour turned out to be wrong.
Who started this rumour?
words.tutor: Tell me two small pieces of news about a shop, one checked and one not, and ask me which is the rumour.

words.meaning: The person or the place a piece of news came from.
words.example: My source was the notice on the door.
practice: She did not name her source.
A good source can be checked.
Where is your source for that?
The source of the news was the driver himself.
words.tutor: Give me a piece of news with no source, and I will ask you the question that turns it into a report.

words.meaning: One person's account of an event, or one form of a thing that has been changed.
words.example: I heard two versions of the story.
practice: Her version of the morning was different from his.
Both versions agree about the time.
Tell me your version.
Do not send the old version of the form.
words.tutor: Describe one small event to me twice, from two different people, and ask me what changed between the versions.

words.meaning: Tell somebody something, in a formal way. It takes a person after it.
words.example: The office informed me about the new time.
practice: Please inform the desk if you cannot come.
They informed us that the road was shut.
Who informed you?
A notice informed everybody of the change.
words.tutor: Read me four sentences with tell in them, and I will say each one again with inform.

words.meaning: Tell somebody again about something they already knew.
words.example: Please remind me on Friday.
practice: She reminded me to bring the form.
Remind him that the shop shuts at six.
This note reminds me of the date.
Who reminded you about the delivery?
words.tutor: Give me three things to do this week, and ask me to remind you about each one in a full sentence.

words.meaning: Say that something is wrong or not good enough.
words.example: He complained about the long wait.
practice: She complained that the food was cold.
You can complain at the desk.
They complained to the driver.
Nobody complained about the new time.
words.tutor: Give me one small problem at a desk, and I will complain about it politely in two sentences.

words.meaning: Say that something is true when nobody has checked it yet.
words.example: He claims that the bus is faster now.
practice: She claimed that she posted it on Monday.
The notice claims the shop opens at eight.
Do not claim more than you know.
What exactly did they claim?
words.tutor: Say four sentences about a shop to me and hide a claim among them, then ask me to point at the claim.

words.meaning: Answer somebody who has spoken or written to you.
words.example: I replied the same day.
practice: She replied that she was busy.
Please reply before Friday.
He read the message and replied at once.
Nobody replied to my note.
words.tutor: Send me three short messages, and ask me to reply to each one in a single sentence.

words.meaning: Say the opposite of what somebody else says, and give a reason.
words.example: They argued about the time for an hour.
practice: He argued that the old route was quicker.
The two neighbours argued about the fence.
Do not argue with the driver.
She argued her case calmly.
words.tutor: Say one ordinary opinion about a bus route, and I will argue the other side in two sentences with a reason.

words.meaning: Say something out loud so that everybody hears it.
words.example: They announced the new opening time.
practice: A voice announced the next stop.
They announced the change on the door.
When did they announce it?
She announced that the group was full.
words.tutor: Give me a change to a shop's opening time, and ask me to announce it in one clear sentence.

words.meaning: Talk to somebody until they change their mind.
words.example: She persuaded me to wait one more day.
practice: He persuaded the shop to change the delivery date.
Nobody could persuade her to stay.
I tried to persuade him, but he said no.
What persuaded you?
words.tutor: Pick an ordinary choice, such as Friday or Monday for a delivery, and let me persuade you to take one of them.

words.meaning: The one before this one.
words.example: The previous bus was full.
practice: I read it in the previous message.
The previous notice gave a different time.
On the previous day, nobody replied.
Her previous answer was clearer than this one.
words.tutor: Give me three notices with dates, and ask me which one is the previous one and which is current.

words.meaning: The one after this one.
words.example: The following day was quiet.
practice: We met again the following week.
She replied the following morning.
The following bus is at ten past.
The following notice was much clearer.
words.tutor: Say four sentences with tomorrow in them, and ask me to report each one with the following day.

words.meaning: From a short time ago.
words.example: That is recent news.
practice: A recent notice changed the opening time.
In recent weeks the bus has been late.
Her most recent message was very short.
Is this a recent version of the form?
words.tutor: Give me two pieces of news, one from today and one from a year ago, and ask me which is recent.

words.meaning: Happening or true now.
words.example: What is the current time of the last bus?
practice: The current notice is on the door.
Her current job is at a clinic.
The current version is the third one.
What is the current opening time?
words.tutor: Give me an old opening time and a new one, and ask me to say which is current and which is former.

words.meaning: From before, and not now.
words.example: A former neighbour told me the news.
practice: That is the former opening time, not the new one.
He is a former driver at the same office.
The former notice is still on the wall.
Her former address is on the old form.
words.tutor: Describe one thing about your week that has changed, and ask me to say the former way and the current way.

words.meaning: Happening with no wait at all.
words.example: The reply was immediate.
practice: The office gave an immediate answer.
There was no immediate news.
An immediate reply saves everybody time.
The immediate problem is the date.
words.tutor: Give me two replies, one after a week and one after a minute, and ask me which one was immediate.

words.meaning: Decide, after thinking about two or more choices. You cannot work this out from the separate words.
words.example: Make up your mind before Friday.
practice: I could not make up my mind about the date.
She made up her mind to reply the same day.
Take a day and make up your mind.
He makes up his mind very quickly.
words.starter: I will make up my mind about …
words.tutor: Give me two dates for a delivery, and ask me to make up my mind out loud and say why.

words.meaning: Watch something while you are doing other things. Nobody's eye moves anywhere.
words.example: Keep an eye on the door.
practice: Could you keep an eye on my bag?
She kept an eye on the clock all morning.
I am keeping an eye on the delivery date.
Keep an eye on the notice board this week.
words.starter: Could you keep an eye on …
words.tutor: Ask me to keep an eye on three different things, and check that I answer each one in a full sentence.

words.meaning: Have none of something left. Nobody runs anywhere.
words.example: We ran out of paper.
practice: The shop has run out of bread.
I ran out of time before the desk shut.
Do not run out of milk again.
They are running out of forms at the office.
words.tutor: Name four things in a kitchen, and ask me to say which ones I have run out of this week.

words.meaning: Do not hurry; use as much time as you need.
words.example: Take your time with the form.
practice: Take your time and read the notice twice.
She took her time over the reply.
There is no queue, so take your time.
He told me to take my time.
words.tutor: Give me a form to fill in out loud, and tell me to take my time, then check that I do not rush the answer.

words.meaning: Because you meant to do it.
words.example: He left the note there on purpose.
practice: I put the form on top on purpose.
Did he do that on purpose?
She kept the old version on purpose.
Nobody breaks a cup on purpose.
words.starter: I did it on purpose because …
words.tutor: Describe two small accidents to me, and ask me which one sounds as if it happened on purpose.

words.meaning: Without meaning to.
words.example: I took the wrong bus by mistake.
practice: She sent the old version by mistake.
He wrote the previous date by mistake.
I deleted the message by mistake.
Anyone can press the wrong button by mistake.
words.tutor: Give me four small everyday errors, and ask me to say each one in a sentence ending by mistake.

grammar.title: Said that, told me that: passing on a statement
grammar.explanation: Somebody says a sentence. Later you pass it on. Add said that or told me that, then step the verb back one step in time. The words inside get no quotation marks, because they are no longer the person's exact words.
grammar.rule:
Direct: 'The shop is shut.'
Reported: She said that the shop was shut.
Direct: 'The bus leaves at six.'
Reported: He said that the bus left at six.
Direct: 'I will ring you.'
Reported: She told me that she would ring me.
Direct: 'I can come on Friday.'
Reported: He told me that he could come on Friday.
The verb steps back one step: is becomes was, are becomes were, leaves becomes left, will becomes would, can becomes could.
Say takes no person: she said that the road was shut.
Tell takes a person: she told me that the road was shut.
The reported sentence takes no quotation marks and no comma.
In speech you may drop that: She said the shop was shut.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The person said: 'The office is closed on Monday.'
Ask: who said it, and who did they say it to?
A woman at the desk said it, and she said it to you.
She said it to you, so you may use told me.
Now step the verb back. Is becomes was.
Take off the quotation marks.
Answer: She told me that the office was closed on Monday.
Or, with no person named: She said that the office was closed on Monday.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write she said me that the office was closed. Say never takes a person straight after it. Write: she told me that the office was closed, or she said that the office was closed.
grammar.tip: Two steps every time. Add said that or told me that, then move the verb back one step.
grammar.practice:
Report each line. Use said that or told me that.
1. The driver: 'The road is shut.'
2. The shop assistant, to you: 'We close at six.'
3. A neighbour: 'The bus leaves at ten past.'
4. The person at the desk, to you: 'I will ring you on Friday.'
5. A colleague: 'I can bring the form today.'
6. The office, to you: 'The date is different now.'
7. A neighbour: 'The café is closing.'
8. The driver, to you: 'I am waiting outside.'
grammar.answers:
1. He said that the road was shut.
2. She told me that they closed at six.
3. She said that the bus left at ten past.
4. He told me that he would ring me on Friday.
5. He said that he could bring the form that day.
6. They told me that the date was different now.
7. She said that the café was closing.
8. He told me that he was waiting outside.
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing she said me that we close at six. Say takes no person, and we becomes they once you are the one reporting.
Item 5 catches people too: can becomes could, and today becomes that day, because you are speaking later.

grammar.title: She told me to wait: passing on an instruction
grammar.explanation: An instruction is not a statement, so it is reported a different way. Use told, then the person, then to, then the plain verb. For a negative instruction, put not in front of to.
grammar.rule:
Direct: 'Wait here.'
Reported: She told me to wait here.
Direct: 'Sign the form.'
Reported: He told me to sign the form.
Direct: 'Do not press that button.'
Reported: She told me not to press that button.
Direct: 'Please ring again on Friday.'
Reported: He asked me to ring again on Friday.
Told is for an instruction. Asked is for a polite request.
The person always comes next: told me, told her, told the driver, told everybody.
The verb after to never changes shape: to wait, to sign, to ring.
Never: she told to wait. Never: she said me to wait.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The notice said: 'Do not leave bags at the desk.'
Ask: is this a statement or an instruction?
It tells somebody to do something, so it is an instruction.
It is negative, so not goes in front of to.
Ask: who was told? Everybody who reads the notice, so you can write me.
Answer: The notice told me not to leave bags at the desk.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to drop the person: she told to wait. Tell always needs somebody after it. Write: she told me to wait.
grammar.tip: Told, then who, then to, then the plain verb. Four steps, always in that order.
grammar.practice:
Report each instruction. Name the person who was told.
1. The driver, to you: 'Wait by the door.'
2. The notice, to everybody: 'Write the time on every slip.'
3. A colleague, to you: 'Do not sign it yet.'
4. The person at the desk, to you: 'Please ring again on Friday.'
5. A neighbour, to you: 'Keep an eye on the parcel.'
6. The office, to you: 'Do not use the old form.'
7. The shop assistant, to you: 'Take your time.'
8. A colleague, to you: 'Remind the driver about the date.'
grammar.answers:
1. He told me to wait by the door.
2. The notice told everybody to write the time on every slip.
3. She told me not to sign it yet.
4. He asked me to ring again on Friday.
5. She told me to keep an eye on the parcel.
6. They told me not to use the old form.
7. She told me to take my time.
8. He told me to remind the driver about the date.
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing she told me to not sign it. Not goes in front of to, never after it.
Item 7 catches people too: your becomes my, because you are the person speaking now.

grammar.title: Tell takes a person, say takes none
grammar.explanation: These two verbs mean almost the same thing and behave differently. Tell needs a person straight after it. Say does not take a person at all, unless you add the word to.
grammar.rule:
Tell, then a person: tell me, tell her, tell the driver, told everybody.
She told me the news. He told the driver the new time.
Say, then the words: say that, say it, say nothing, say hello.
She said that the road was shut. He said nothing for a moment.
Add to if you want a person after say: she said it to me.
Fixed pairs with tell: tell the truth, tell a story, tell the time, tell a lie.
Fixed pairs with say: say sorry, say hello, say goodbye, say a word.
Never: she said me. Never: she told that.
Inform works like tell: the office informed me that the date was different.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The item: The office ____ me that the date was different.
Ask: is there a person straight after the gap?
Yes. Me is a person.
So the verb must be one that can take a person.
Tell can. Say cannot.
Answer: The office told me that the date was different.
Inform also fits here: The office informed me that the date was different.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write he said me the time. Say cannot hold a person on its own. Write: he told me the time, or he said the time to me.
grammar.tip: If a person comes next, use tell. If words come next, use say.
grammar.practice:
Write said or told in each gap.
1. She ____ me that the shop was shut.
2. He ____ that the bus was late.
3. Nobody ____ us about the change.
4. The driver ____ nothing.
5. They ____ everybody to wait outside.
6. She ____ hello and sat down.
7. The notice ____ that the office was closed.
8. Who ____ you that?
grammar.answers:
1. told 2. said 3. told 4. said 5. told 6. said 7. said 8. told
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing said. Us is a person, and say cannot take one on its own.
Item 7 catches people the other way round: nothing sits between the verb and that, so it is said. A notice can also tell somebody, but only if a person follows it.

grammar.title: I need you to sign it. I have calls to make.
grammar.explanation: Two patterns here, and both put the small word to in front of a plain verb. To ask for a job to be done, use the verb, then the person, then to. To list a job that is still waiting, use have, then the thing, then to.
grammar.rule:
I need you to sign it.
She wants me to come early.
They asked him to wait at the desk.
I would like you to check the date.
The shape is the same every time: verb, person, to, plain verb.
Now the second pattern.
I have three calls to make.
She has a form to fill in.
He has nothing to do until Friday.
We have one more question to ask.
The shape is: have, the thing, to, plain verb.
Both patterns keep the verb plain after to: to sign, to make, to fill in.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want the driver to ring again on Friday.
Start with what you need: I need.
Then the person: I need the driver.
Then to, then the plain verb: I need the driver to ring again on Friday.
Now add your own waiting job in the same sentence.
The job is a form. The plain verb is sign.
Answer: I need the driver to ring again on Friday, and I have a form to sign.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to drop the person: I need to sign it, when you mean somebody else. That sentence says you will sign it yourself. Write: I need you to sign it.
grammar.tip: Ask two questions. Who does it, and what is the plain verb? Put to between them.
grammar.practice:
Build one sentence from each set of words.
1. I / need / you / sign / the form
2. She / wants / me / come / at nine
3. They / asked / him / wait / outside
4. I / have / two calls / make / before lunch
5. He / has / a form / fill in / today
6. We / have / nothing / do / until Friday
7. The office / needs / us / reply / before Friday
8. I / would like / you / check / the date
grammar.answers:
1. I need you to sign the form.
2. She wants me to come at nine.
3. They asked him to wait outside.
4. I have two calls to make before lunch.
5. He has a form to fill in today.
6. We have nothing to do until Friday.
7. The office needs us to reply before Friday.
8. I would like you to check the date.
The likeliest wrong answer is 4: writing I have two calls for make. The word in front of the plain verb is always to.
Item 7 catches people too: needs keeps its s, because the office is one thing, like he or she.

grammar.title: The day before, later that week, straight away
grammar.explanation: A report almost always says when. Once you are reporting, the time word moves with you: yesterday becomes the day before, and tomorrow becomes the next day. A report with no time in it is hard to check.
grammar.rule:
At the moment of speaking: yesterday. In your report: the day before.
At the moment of speaking: today. In your report: that day.
At the moment of speaking: tomorrow. In your report: the next day, or the following day.
At the moment of speaking: last week. In your report: the previous week.
At the moment of speaking: now. In your report: at that moment.
She said that the road was shut the day before.
He told me that he would ring the following morning.
The office replied straight away. Straight away means at once, with no wait.
Other time words you will read and hear: earlier that morning, later that week, recently, previously, immediately, currently.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
On Tuesday the driver said: 'I rang yesterday.'
You are reporting it on Thursday.
Ask: which day is yesterday, for the driver?
It is Monday, the day before he spoke.
If you keep the word yesterday, it now points at Wednesday, which is the wrong day.
So change it: the day before.
Answer: He said that he rang the day before.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to keep the speaker's own word: he said that he rang yesterday. Two days later, yesterday means a different day. Write: he said that he rang the day before.
grammar.tip: Move the time word with you. Yesterday becomes the day before; tomorrow becomes the next day.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing time word.
1. On Monday she said: 'I posted it yesterday.' She said that she posted it ____ .
2. On Monday he said: 'I will ring tomorrow.' He told me that he would ring ____ .
3. The office answered at once. The answer was ____ .
4. The bus in front of this one was full. The ____ bus was full.
5. The week after that one was quieter. The ____ week was quieter.
6. The news came two days ago. It is ____ news.
7. That was her job before, and it is not now. It is her ____ job.
8. This is the notice on the door today. It is the ____ notice.
grammar.answers:
1. the day before 2. the following day, or the next day 3. immediate 4. previous 5. following 6. recent 7. former 8. current
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing yesterday. Yesterday points at the day before you speak, not the day before she spoke.
Item 8 catches people too: current means now, while recent means from a short time ago. A current notice is up today; a recent notice may already be down.

readings.title: The message at the desk
readings.setting: A front desk, and the stairs ten minutes later
readings.passage:
Priya is at the front desk. The man behind it is holding a note.
'Your delivery is not coming today,' he says. 'The driver rang earlier this morning. He said that the road was shut.'
'Shut? Since when?'
'Since the previous night. There are roadworks. He told me to ask you for a new date.'
Priya takes out her diary.
'Friday,' she says. 'Can you tell him Friday?'
'I will. And he asked me to remind you about the form. He needs you to sign it before he brings anything.'
'I have the form somewhere. I have two calls to make first, then I will find it.'
'Take your time. Nothing moves before Friday now.'
Ten minutes later Priya meets a neighbour on the stairs.
'Any news?' the neighbour asks.
'The delivery is not coming,' says Priya. 'The man at the desk told me that the road was shut. The driver rang earlier this morning.'
'I heard something different. Somebody said that the shop was closing.'
'That is a rumour,' says Priya. 'My source is the driver himself. That is the version I believe.'
'Fair enough. So what happens now?'
'They told me to sign the form and wait. The new date is Friday.'
'Straight away, or later that week?'
'Friday, the man said. Not the following week.'
The neighbour writes the date on the back of her hand and goes down the stairs.

readings.title: Passing a message on so that it survives
readings.setting: Any desk where messages are taken for other people
readings.passage:
A message changes shape a little every time it moves. That is normal, and it is why a report needs care.
Start with the source. The source is the person or the place the news came from. If you cannot name the source, say so. A story with no source is a rumour, not news.
Next, keep the statement and your own words apart. A statement is what the person actually said. Your report is your account of it. Keep the two apart in your head, and your report stays honest.
Then choose the verb. Say does not take a person after it, so you write: she said that the road was shut. Tell does take a person: she told me that the road was shut. Inform is the formal word, and you will see it on notices and in offices.
Now the time. Almost every report needs to say when. The driver rang earlier that morning. The office replied the following day. The answer was immediate. Straight away means at once, with no wait in between. A report with no time in it is hard for anybody to check.
Watch out for two versions of one event. Two people can be honest and still disagree, because each of them noticed something different. When you hear two versions, report both, and name the source of each.
A headline is the shortest report there is. It carries the subject and nothing else. An announcement is the loudest: one message, many people, one moment.
Finally, check before you pass anything on. Was it a statement or a claim? A claim is something nobody has checked yet. One question at the desk is usually enough, and it stops a rumour before it starts.

readings.title: While you were out
readings.setting: A pad of message slips beside a front desk
readings.passage:
WHILE YOU WERE OUT
Message for: Ana, desk 4
Taken by: Sam
Date: Tuesday 14 March
Time: 9.40 in the morning

Caller: the delivery driver
Telephone: 20 84 51

MESSAGE
He said that the road was shut for roadworks.
He told me to ask you for a new date.
He needs you to sign the form before the next delivery.
He will ring again the following morning.

ACTION NEEDED: yes
URGENT: no
Return the call before 5 in the afternoon.

NOTICE FOR EVERYONE WHO TAKES A MESSAGE AT THIS DESK
Write the time on every slip. A message with no time on it cannot be checked.
Name the caller. If you did not catch the name, write not given. Do not guess.
Write what the caller said, not what you think they meant.
If a caller gives two different times, write both. Do not choose one for them.
Pass the slip on straight away. Do not keep it in a pocket.
If the caller asks for an immediate answer, ring the desk manager on 20 84 60.
Keep the previous week's slips in the box under the desk for one month.
One slip, one caller. If a second person rings, start a new slip.
Write an instruction as an instruction: he told me to ring back, not he wants to talk.
If the caller says something you did not catch, ask them to say it again before they ring off.
A slip nobody can read is a slip nobody acts on, so write the numbers slowly.

comprehension.q: What reason did the driver give for not coming today?
comprehension.a: He said that the road was shut, because of roadworks.
comprehension.why: The man at the desk reports it twice: he said that the road was shut, and then, since the previous night, there are roadworks.

comprehension.q: What does the driver want Priya to do before the next delivery?
comprehension.a: He needs her to sign the form.
comprehension.why: The man says: he needs you to sign it before he brings anything. It is the form he asked the man to remind her about.

comprehension.q: The man says 'Take your time.' What is he telling Priya?
comprehension.a: That she does not need to hurry.
comprehension.why: He says it straight after she says she has two calls to make first. Nothing can move before Friday, so there is no hurry. The saying is not about taking anything.

comprehension.q: Why does Priya call the neighbour's story a rumour?
comprehension.a: Because nobody has checked it, and it does not match her own source.
comprehension.why: The neighbour heard that the shop was closing and cannot say where from. Priya's news came from the driver himself, so she has a source and the neighbour does not.

comprehension.q: Priya now has the new date. What are the two things she said she would do first?
comprehension.a: Make two calls, and then find the form.
comprehension.why: She says: I have two calls to make first, then I will find it. The form is what she is looking for.

comprehension.q: According to this text, what is a story with no source?
comprehension.why: The text says it in one line: a story with no source is a rumour, not news. Naming the source is the first step it gives.

comprehension.q: Which verb takes a person straight after it, say or tell?
comprehension.why: The text gives both forms. She said that the road was shut has no person. She told me that the road was shut has me straight after the verb.

comprehension.q: The text says two honest people can give two different versions. Why?
comprehension.a: Because each of them noticed something different.
comprehension.why: The text gives the reason in the same sentence. Being honest is about what you noticed, so two honest accounts can still disagree.

comprehension.q: You are Ana. By when must you return the call, and which number do you ring?
comprehension.why: The slip says return the call before 5 in the afternoon, and the caller's telephone number is 20 84 51. The other number, 20 84 60, is the desk manager's.

comprehension.q: You take a call and you do not catch the caller's name. What does the notice tell you to write?
comprehension.a: Write not given. Do not guess.
comprehension.why: The notice gives that instruction in one line. A guessed name looks like a fact on the slip, and the next reader has no way of knowing it was a guess.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — She said that, she told me that
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
She said that the shop was shut.
She told me that the shop was shut.
He said that the bus left at ten past.
He told me that he would ring on Friday.
They said that the date was different.
They told me that the date was different.
The office said that the form was ready.
The office informed me that the form was ready.
Now make eight of your own, about an ordinary week. You may invent every detail.
Play back your recording.
Check one thing: after said there is no person, and after told there is one.
Say any line again if a person has crept in after said.
speaking.tutor: Say six reported sentences to me, some with said and some with told, and tell me if any of them puts a person after said.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Passing on an instruction
speaking.instructions:
Read each instruction, then say the report out loud.
Wait by the door. She told me to wait by the door.
Sign the form. He told me to sign the form.
Do not press that button. She told me not to press that button.
Please ring again on Friday. He asked me to ring again on Friday.
Do not use the old version. They told me not to use the old version.
Take your time. She told me to take my time.
Now record all six reports, one after the other.
Play them back and count the words between told and to.
Check: there should be exactly one, and it should be a person.
Me, her, him, the driver, everybody. Any of those is right.
If told sits straight next to to anywhere, record that line again.
speaking.tutor: Give me six short instructions, one at a time, and I will report each one back with told me to or asked me to.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, or tell me
speaking.instructions:
Read each question, then answer it out loud with the verb it needs.
What did the notice say? Answer with say: It said that the office was closed.
What did the driver tell you? Answer with tell: He told me that the road was shut.
What did you say at the desk? Answer with say: I said sorry and asked for a new date.
What did the office inform you about? Answer with inform: They informed me that the form was ready.
What did nobody tell you? Answer with tell: Nobody told me about the change.
Record the five answers and play them back.
Check: every tell and every inform in your answers has a person straight after it.
Check: no say in your answers has a person straight after it.
Say any answer again if one of the two checks fails.
speaking.tutor: Ask me five questions about a message I was given, and stop me whenever I put a person straight after say.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Asking through somebody else
speaking.instructions:
You are at a desk. Say each line out loud, then say what you still have to do.
I need you to sign this form. I have two calls to make.
I would like you to check the date. I have one more question to ask.
I need the driver to ring me before ten. I have a form to fill in.
I want the office to send the current version. I have nothing to do until Friday.
Now make four of your own. Use a real errand or an invented one.
Each one is two sentences: what you need from somebody else, then what is still waiting for you.
Record the four pairs and play them back.
Check: the word to sits in front of every plain verb.
Check: a person comes after need, want, would like and ask.
speaking.tutor: Play the person behind a desk. I will ask you to do three jobs for me, and you tell me whether each request was clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — When was it said?
speaking.instructions:
Say each report out loud, and put the time word in the right place.
She said that she posted it the day before.
He told me that he would ring the following morning.
They replied straight away.
The previous notice gave a different time.
The current opening time is on the door.
Her former address is still on the old form.
The news is recent, so the source is easy to check.
Now report one real message from your own week, or one you invent.
Say who spoke to you, when they spoke, and what they said.
Record it and play it back.
Check: count the time words. There should be at least two.
If there are none, record it again with the day before and straight away in it.
speaking.tutor: Give me four short reports with no time words in them, and ask me to say each one again with a time word added.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Give the message back
speaking.instructions:
Listen to the lesson for this unit again, from the part about the time words to the end.
It uses two phrases you may not know: straight away, and make up your mind.
Do not stop the lesson to look them up. Listen to the words around each phrase and write down what you think each one means.
Then check your two guesses against the word cards for this unit.
Now play the lesson once more and stop it after the six sayings.
Record a summary of one minute. Say three things the lesson told you to do.
Start like this: The lesson said that a report needs a time in it.
Then: It told me to move the time word with me.
Play your recording back.
Check: three reported sentences, at least one with said that and at least one with told me to.
If one is missing, record the summary again.
speaking.tutor: Say a short telephone message to me twice, then ask me to give it back to you in two reported sentences.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Four reports
writing.prompt: Four people spoke to you this week. Write one reported sentence for each. You may invent all four. Use said that twice and told me that twice.
writing.model:
The shop assistant said that the delivery was coming on Friday.
The driver told me that he would ring before ten.
A neighbour said that the café was closing.
The office told me that the old form was no longer in use.
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Two use said that and two use told me that. No quotation marks anywhere. Every verb has stepped back one step: is to was, will to would, opens to opened. Every sentence ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Do one first. Write the person's exact line inside quotation marks. Then take the quotation marks off, add said that, and change is to was. The sentence is finished.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence that reports an instruction instead of a statement, starting: she told me to.

writing.title: Writing 2 — The message slip
writing.prompt: You took a telephone call for somebody else. Write a message slip, using the layout of Reading 3. Invent the caller and the whole message. Report at least one statement and at least one instruction.
writing.model:
WHILE YOU WERE OUT
Message for: Eva, desk 2
Taken by: Ben
Date: Thursday 6 June
Time: 11.15 in the morning
Caller: the clinic
MESSAGE
They said that the appointment was moving to the following week.
They told me to ring back before four.
ACTION NEEDED: yes
writing.starter:
WHILE YOU WERE OUT
Message for:
writing.criteria: Nine lines. A date line and a time line. At least one message line with said that or told me that. At least one message line with told me to. One line saying whether action is needed.
writing.support: Copy the six headings from Reading 3 first, in order, and leave the message part empty. Then fill the headings in one at a time. The message itself needs only two lines.
writing.extension: Add one line naming the source of the news, and one line saying whether the caller wanted an immediate answer.

writing.title: Writing 3 — What I was told
writing.prompt: Write two short paragraphs about a message somebody gave you. You may invent all of it. In the first paragraph, say who spoke to you, when they spoke, and what they said. In the second, say what you did about it. Join your sentences with and, but, so, because, then, after that and however.
writing.model:
On Tuesday morning the person at the desk told me that my delivery was not coming. She said that the road was shut, because there were roadworks. She also told me to ask for a new date. The driver rang earlier that morning, so the news was recent and the source was good.

I made up my mind straight away. I rang the office and asked them to book Friday, because I was free that day. They replied the same afternoon and told me not to use the old form. However, I could not find the new one, so I still have one more call to make.
writing.length: Two paragraphs, four to six sentences each
writing.criteria: Two paragraphs with an empty line between them. At least three reported sentences using said that, told me that or told me to. At least four joining words from the list. At least one time word from this unit in each paragraph. Every sentence ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Write the first paragraph as four separate short sentences with no joining words at all. Then join two of the pairs, one with so and one with because. That paragraph is now finished.
writing.extension: Add a third paragraph reporting a second version of the same news, and name the source of each version.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Six sayings, six lines
writing.prompt: Write six lines about one ordinary week. Use one saying in each line: make up your mind, keep an eye on, run out of, take your time, on purpose, by mistake. You may invent the whole week.
writing.model:
On Monday I ran out of milk before breakfast.
On Tuesday I took the wrong bus by mistake.
On Wednesday I could not make up my mind about the delivery date.
On Thursday a neighbour asked me to keep an eye on a parcel.
On Friday the person at the desk told me to take my time with the form.
On Saturday I left the old version on the shelf on purpose, so that I could compare the two.
writing.criteria: Six lines. A different saying in each line. Each saying written whole, with no word changed inside it, except my, her or his in make up your mind and take your time. Every line ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Start with the two easiest, run out of and by mistake. Copy the shape of the model line and change only the last few words.
writing.extension: Write two more lines, each holding two of the sayings in one sentence. Then read all eight out loud.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: statement, news, report, announcement, headline, rumour, source, version.
1. The short line at the top of a story is the ____ .
2. A story that nobody has checked is only a ____ .
3. The person the news came from is the ____ .
4. She gave a short ____ about the delay, and then answered questions.
5. Her ____ of the morning was different from his.
6. The ____ about the new bus route is good.
7. There was an ____ over the speaker about the late train.
8. He wrote a two-page ____ about what happened.
activities.answers:
1. headline 2. rumour 3. source 4. statement 5. version 6. news 7. announcement 8. report
Eight out of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the word cards for the ones you missed. Five or fewer: read all eight cards again, then do this once more.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck, and mark which ones needed it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Say, tell or inform?
activities.instructions:
Write said, told, tell or informed in each gap. Read the whole sentence before you choose.
1. She ____ me that the date was different.
2. He ____ that the road was shut.
3. Please ____ the driver about the new time.
4. The office ____ me that the form was ready.
5. Nobody ____ anything for a moment.
6. Can you ____ me the time?
7. They ____ that the shop opens at eight.
8. I ____ sorry and sat down.
activities.answers:
1. told 2. said 3. tell 4. informed 5. said 6. tell 7. said 8. said
Seven or eight: move on. Five or six: read grammar card 3 again and redo items 1, 4 and 6. Four or fewer: do the card 3 practice first, then come back.
The two that catch most people are 4 and 5. Informed takes a person, like told. Said nothing is a fixed pair, so nothing may follow said with no person in between.
activities.solo: Put your finger over the gap and read the words that come after it. If the next word is a person, the answer is told, tell or informed.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Report the line
activities.instructions:
Write each line as a report. Use said that or told me that.
1. The shop assistant, to you: 'The delivery is on Friday.'
2. A neighbour: 'The café is closing at the end of the month.'
3. The driver, to you: 'I will come before ten.'
4. The office: 'The old form is no longer in use.'
5. A colleague, to you: 'I can check it this afternoon.'
6. The notice: 'The lift is out of use.'
activities.answers:
1. She told me that the delivery was on Friday.
2. He said that the café was closing at the end of the month.
3. He told me that he would come before ten.
4. They said that the old form was no longer in use.
5. She told me that she could check it that afternoon.
6. It said that the lift was out of use.
Five or six: move on. Three or four: check whether you stepped the verb back each time. Two or fewer: read grammar card 1 again and redo all six.
Items 3 and 5 are the test: will becomes would, and can becomes could.
activities.solo: Write the exact line first, inside quotation marks. Then cross the quotation marks out and change the verb. Working in two steps is faster than working in one.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Told me to, needs me to
activities.instructions:
Write each one as a report.
1. The driver, to you: 'Wait by the gate.'
2. A colleague, to you: 'Do not send the old version.'
3. The office needs this from you: you sign the form.
4. Your neighbour wants this from you: you keep an eye on a parcel.
5. The notice, to everybody: 'Write the time on every slip.'
6. You still have these jobs waiting: two calls, one form.
activities.answers:
1. He told me to wait by the gate.
2. She told me not to send the old version.
3. The office needs me to sign the form.
4. My neighbour wants me to keep an eye on a parcel.
5. The notice told everybody to write the time on every slip.
6. I have two calls to make and one form to sign.
Five or six: move on. Three or four: check that a person sits between the verb and to in every one. Two or fewer: read grammar cards 2 and 4 again.
Item 2 is the test: not goes in front of to, so it is not to send, never to not send.
activities.solo: Say each answer out loud before you write it. The missing person is much easier to hear than to see.

activities.title: Practice 5 — When was it said?
activities.instructions:
Write the missing time word.
Use: the day before, the following day, straight away, previous, recent, current, former, immediate.
1. On Friday she said: 'I rang yesterday.' She said that she rang ____ .
2. On Friday he said: 'I will write tomorrow.' He told me that he would write ____ .
3. The answer came with no wait at all. It was ____ .
4. He replied at once, with nothing in between. He replied ____ .
5. That was the notice before this one. It is the ____ notice.
6. She had that job before, and she does not now. It is her ____ job.
7. The news came three days ago. It is ____ news.
8. This is the time printed on the door today. It is the ____ opening time.
activities.answers:
1. the day before 2. the following day 3. immediate 4. straight away 5. previous 6. former 7. recent 8. current
Seven or eight: move on. Five or six: read grammar card 5 again and redo items 1 and 2. Four or fewer: do the card 5 practice first, then come back.
Items 3 and 4 look the same and are not. Immediate describes the answer, so it goes in front of a noun. Straight away describes when he replied, so it goes after the verb.
activities.solo: Do items 5 to 8 first. They are single words in front of a noun, and they will warm you up for the two reports at the top.

activities.title: Practice 6 — What does the saying mean?
activities.instructions:
Match each saying to its meaning. Write the letter.
Sayings:
1. make up your mind
2. keep an eye on
3. run out of
4. take your time
5. on purpose
6. by mistake
Meanings:
a. do not hurry
b. have none of it left
c. because you meant to
d. decide
e. without meaning to
f. watch it while you do other things
Then write one sentence of your own for two of the six sayings.
activities.answers:
1 d, 2 f, 3 b, 4 a, 5 c, 6 e
Six out of six: move on. Four or five: read the two word cards you missed and try again tomorrow. Three or fewer: read all six cards, then redo it.
The last part is open. Check two things in your own sentences: the saying is written whole, and no word inside it has been changed. For example: I ran out of forms before lunch. Not: I ran out from forms.
activities.solo: Cover the meanings and say what you think each saying means. Then uncover them and match. Guessing first is what makes the matching stick.

quizzes.q: A shop assistant said: 'The shop is shut.' Which sentence reports it correctly?
options: She said that the shop was shut.
She said me that the shop was shut.
She told that the shop was shut.
She said to that the shop was shut.
quizzes.a: She said that the shop was shut.
quizzes.why: Say takes that and then a whole sentence, with the verb stepped back: is becomes was. She said me is the tempting one, because tell does take a person there; say never does. She told that is the same error the other way round, with the person missing. The last one adds a stray to.

quizzes.q: The driver said: 'I will ring you.' How do you report it?
options: The driver told me that he will ring me.
The driver told me that he would ring me.
The driver said me that he would ring me.
The driver told me would ring me.
quizzes.a: The driver told me that he would ring me.
quizzes.why: Will steps back to would in a report. The first option keeps will, which is the commonest error here. The third puts a person after said, and say cannot take one. The fourth has lost its subject, he.

quizzes.q: A colleague said: 'Wait by the door.' How do you report it?
options: She told me wait by the door.
She said me to wait by the door.
She told me to wait by the door.
She told to wait by the door.
quizzes.a: She told me to wait by the door.
quizzes.why: An instruction is reported with told, then the person, then to, then the plain verb. The first option drops to. The second uses say, which cannot take a person. The fourth drops the person, and tell always needs one.

quizzes.q: Which sentence reports the instruction 'Do not press that button'?
options: She told me to not press that button.
She told me do not press that button.
She said me not to press that button.
She told me not to press that button.
quizzes.a: She told me not to press that button.
quizzes.why: Not goes in front of to. The first option is the tempting one, because it keeps the words in the order you hear them; English puts not before to here. The second leaves the direct instruction unchanged. The third uses say with a person after it.

quizzes.q: Which word fits? The office ____ me that the form was ready.
options: said
told
spoke
answered
quizzes.why: Me is a person, and it sits straight after the gap, so the verb must be one that takes a person there. Told does. Said is the tempting one, because the rest of the sentence fits it perfectly; it fails only on the person. Spoke needs to before a person, and answered does not take that and a sentence in this way.

options: He said me the time.
He told the time.
He said to me the time.
He told me the time.
quizzes.why: Tell the time is a fixed pair, and tell takes a person first. Said me puts a person after say. Told the time with no person leaves tell incomplete. Said to me the time has the right pieces in the wrong order: he said the time to me would be correct.

quizzes.q: You want the driver to ring on Friday. What do you say?
options: I need you to ring on Friday.
I need to ring on Friday.
I need you ring on Friday.
I need that you ring on Friday.
quizzes.a: I need you to ring on Friday.
quizzes.why: The shape is verb, person, to, plain verb. The second option is the trap: it is a correct English sentence, but it says that you will do the ringing. The third drops to, and the fourth uses that, which this pattern never takes.

quizzes.q: Which sentence says that a job is still waiting for you?
options: I have made three calls.
I am making three calls.
I have three calls to make.
I have three calls for make.
quizzes.a: I have three calls to make.
quizzes.why: Have, then the thing, then to, then the plain verb. The first option says the calls are finished, which is the opposite. The second says you are on the telephone now. The fourth uses for, and the word in front of a plain verb here is always to.

quizzes.q: On Monday she said: 'I posted it yesterday.' You report it on Wednesday. Which is right?
options: She said that she posted it yesterday.
She said that she posts it yesterday.
She said that she will post it the day before.
She said that she posted it the day before.
quizzes.a: She said that she posted it the day before.
quizzes.why: Yesterday moves with the speaker, so in your report it becomes the day before. The first option keeps yesterday, which now points at Tuesday rather than Sunday. The second mixes a present verb with a past time word. The third turns a finished action into a future one.

quizzes.q: Which word means from a short time ago?
options: recent
current
former
immediate
quizzes.why: Recent is about a short distance back in time. Current is the tempting one, because recent news and current news feel close; current means now, and a recent notice may already have been taken down. Former means before and not now. Immediate means with no wait at all.

quizzes.q: A story that is going round, that nobody has checked, is a
options: headline
statement
rumour
source
quizzes.why: A rumour is exactly that: unchecked, and moving from person to person. A headline is the short line at the top of a story, checked or not. A statement is something a person actually said. A source is the person or place news came from, which is what a rumour has none of.

quizzes.q: Somebody says 'Take your time.' What are they telling you?
options: Decide quickly.
There is no need to hurry.
You have run out of time.
Watch the clock for me.
quizzes.a: There is no need to hurry.
quizzes.why: The saying means use as much time as you need. The third option is the tempting one, because the separate words point at time running short; the saying means the opposite. The first is what make up your mind can mean, and the fourth is close to keep an eye on.

teacherNotes.note: Say and tell is the error that survives longest, and it is not a meaning problem. Both verbs mean the same thing to the learner, so explaining the difference again does not help. What helps is a shape: put a finger on the word straight after the verb and ask, is that a person? If yes, it must be tell or inform. Two rounds of Practice 2 done that way usually fixes it for good.

Stepping the verb back feels dishonest to many learners, because the shop really is still shut. It is worth saying plainly that English does this whether the fact has changed or not, and that a learner who keeps the present form will still be understood. It is a habit to build, not a rule that has to be believed.

Reporting a negative instruction produces she told me to not press it, from almost everybody, on the first attempt. It sounds reasonable and it is the order the direct instruction has. The fix is to read the correct version out loud three times rather than to explain it, because the ear settles this one faster than the eye. Quiz item 4 is built on it.

The six everyday sayings cannot be worked out from their separate words, and a learner who tries to will get every one of them wrong. Practice 6 asks for a guess before the meanings are uncovered on purpose: the guess makes the real meaning stick. Do not correct a wrong guess at that stage; let the matching do it.

The tutor is a rehearsal partner in this unit, not a marking service. It is useful for giving instructions to report back, for playing the person behind a desk in Speaking 4, and for reading a short message twice so that the learner can summarise it. Every task here carries its own answer key or its own checklist, so nothing in the unit depends on the tutor's opinion.

selfAssessment.statement: I can write down what somebody said, using said that or told me that.
I can tell somebody what I was asked or told to do.
I can choose say or tell correctly in a sentence.
I can ask somebody to do something for me and say what I still have to do.
I can say when a message was given to me, and pass on the details.
I can write two short paragraphs about a message, with my sentences joined.
I can read an everyday saying and work out what it means.
I can listen to a short message and say the important parts back.

assignment.title: The message I was given
assignment.instructions:
Make one recording and write one short account. You may invent every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about one minute.
Somebody gave you a message this week. Pass it on out loud.
Say who spoke to you and when they spoke: use one time word from this unit.
Report what they said: use said that once and told me that once.
Report what they asked you to do: use told me to or asked me to once.
Say what you need from somebody else: use I need you to once.
Say what is still waiting for you: use I have something to do once.
End with one of the six sayings.
Play the recording back and count the six things in the list above.
If one is missing, record it again. Do not correct it in your head.
Part 2. The written account.
Write two paragraphs, four to six sentences each, about the same message.
Paragraph one: who spoke, when, and what they said.
Paragraph two: what you did about it, and what is still waiting.
Join your sentences with and, but, so, because, then, after that and however.
Under the two paragraphs, write one line that starts: This shows I can …
Check your account against the five criteria for Writing 3 before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and a written account
